translations.text:
Chapter 1.

When the king of the Chaldeans took the Israelites captive, God spoke to Jeremiah and said to him, “Jeremiah, my chosen one, arise and leave this city, you and Baruch, for I am about to destroy it because of the many sins of those who live in it. Your prayer is like a strong pillar in the middle of the city and like a wall of adamant around it. Now arise, go, and leave before the army of the Chaldeans comes and surrounds the city.”

Jeremiah spoke, saying, “I beg you, my Lord, allow your servant to speak before you.” God said to him, “Speak, Jeremiah, my chosen one.”

Jeremiah spoke and said, “Lord, who holds all things, will you hand over this chosen city to the Chaldeans, so that the king may boast with his people and say, ‘I have conquered the city of God’? Far be it, Lord! If this is your will, destroy it with your own hand.”

The Lord said to Jeremiah, “Since you are my chosen one, arise and leave, you and Baruch, for I am about to destroy it because of the sins of those who live in it. Neither the king nor his army can enter the city unless I go before them and open its gates. Now arise, go to Baruch, and tell him this message. At the sixth hour of the night, get up and come to the city wall, and I will show you. Unless I first destroy the city, they cannot enter it.” Having said this, the Lord departed from Jeremiah.

Chapter 2.

Then Jeremiah tore his clothes, put dust on his head, and entered the temple. When Baruch saw Jeremiah with his head covered in dirt and his clothes torn, he cried out loudly, saying, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you, and what sin have the people committed?” For whenever the people sinned, Jeremiah would grieve, put dust on his head, and pray for the people until their wrongdoing was forgiven.

Baruch asked him, saying, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you, and what has happened to the people?”

Jeremiah said to him, “Take care that we do not tear our clothes, but rather tear our hearts. Let us not put water in the basins, so that we may weep fully until we fill them with tears, for from now on no mercy will be shown to these people.”

Baruch said, “My father Jeremiah, what has happened to you?” Jeremiah said to him, “God will hand the city over to the king of the Chaldeans, for he will cruelly take the people captive.”

When Baruch heard all this, he tore his clothes and said, “My father Jeremiah, what message was sent to you?” Jeremiah said to him, “Stay with me until the sixth hour of the night, so that you may know the true message.” And they remained in the temple, weeping.

Part 3.

When it was the sixth hour of the night, the Lord told Jeremiah to go out with Baruch. They reached the city wall and sat waiting. A horn sounded, and angels came out of heaven, carrying fiery lights in their hands, and stood at the city wall. Then Jeremiah and Baruch wept, saying, “Now we know that the matter is true.”

Jeremiah pleaded with the angels, saying, “I beg you all, do not destroy the city until I ask God one thing.” The Lord spoke to the angels, saying, “Do not destroy the city until I speak with Jeremiah, my chosen one.”

Then Jeremiah spoke, saying, “I beg you, my Lord, allow me to speak with you.” He said to him, “Speak whatever you wish, Jeremiah, my chosen one.”

Jeremiah said to him, “Look, now we know, my Lord, that you will hand the city over to its enemies and that the people from Babylon will capture it. What do you wish me to do with the holy things of our service, with which we serve in secret? What do you wish me to do with them?”

The Lord said to him, “Take them and entrust them to the earth and to the temple, saying, ‘You, earth, listen to the voice of your Creator, who created you by the power of the waters and sealed you with seven seals. Surrender your beauty and guard the vessels of your service until the coming of the Beloved.’”

Jeremiah spoke and said, “I beg you, my Lord, show me what I should do for Abimelech the Ethiopian. He has greatly protected the people, and your servant Jeremiah more than all the people of the city. He brought me out of the muddy pit. I do not wish him to see the city's ruin and destruction, so that he will not grieve.”

The Lord said to Jeremiah, “Send him to Agrippa's vineyard by the mountain road, and I will shelter him until I bring the people back into the city. But you, Jeremiah, go with the people until you reach the land of Babylon, and remain there prophesying to them until I bring them back into their city. Leave Baruch here in Jerusalem.”

The Lord told Jeremiah all this and departed from Jeremiah into heaven. Jeremiah and Baruch entered the temple and entrusted all the vessels of their service to the earth, as the Lord had commanded them. Then the earth swallowed them, and the two of them sat and wept.

Early the next morning, Jeremiah sent Abimelech away, saying, “Take a basket and go by the mountain road to Agrippa's vineyard. Bring a few figs for the sick among the people, for the Lord's joy and his glory rest upon your head.” He went as Jeremiah had commanded him.

Part 4.

Early the next morning, the Chaldean army surrounded the city. An angel blew a great horn and said, “Enter, army of the Chaldeans! Look, the gates are opening for you.” Then the king entered with his army, and they took all the people captive.

Then Jeremiah took the keys of the temple and went outside the city. He threw these keys toward the sun, saying, “To you I speak, sun: take the keys of God's house and guard them until the time when God asks you for them. For our birth has not made us worthy to guard it, since we have been found wanting because of our sins.”

While Jeremiah was weeping for the people, they brought him out, dragging him, and drove him along with the people as far as Babylon.

But Baruch took dust and put it on his head. He sat down and uttered this lament, saying, “Why has Jerusalem been ruined, except because of the sin of the beloved people? She has been handed over to her enemy because of our sins and those of the people. But let sinners not boast and say, ‘We were able to capture God's city by our own strength.’ It was not by your might that you overcame her; rather, because of our sins she was handed over to you. Our God will have mercy on us and bring us back into our city, but for you there is no life. Blessed are our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, for they departed from this world and did not see the ruin of this city.”

After saying this, he went out weeping and said, “I grieve for you, Jerusalem.” He left the city and stayed among the tombs, and angels came and told him about everything.

Part 5.

At noon, Abimelech brought figs from the place to which Jeremiah had sent him. He found a leafy tree and sat in its shade to rest a little. He rested his head on the basket of figs and slept for sixty-six years without waking from his sleep.

After these days, he rose and awoke from his sleep and said, “If only I could sleep a little longer, for my head is still heavy and I have not had enough sleep.” He opened that basket of figs and found the figs fresh and dripping milky sap. He wanted to sleep again, because his head was heavy and he had not had enough sleep. But he said, “I am afraid to sleep or doze, lest my father Jeremiah rebuke me, for he sent me away in haste early in the morning. Now I will get up and go, for the heat is intense and never lets up anywhere.”

He got up, took his basket of figs, and entered the city of Jerusalem. He did not recognize the city or his house, and he said, “Blessed are you, Lord,” for great bewilderment had come over him. He said, “Is this not the city of Jerusalem? Surely I am mistaken, although I came by the mountain road. Or perhaps it is because my head is heavy, I have not had enough sleep, and my mind has forgotten. How will I tell Jeremiah about this matter—that the city has become strange to me?”

He searched for every landmark in the city to learn whether it really was Jerusalem. He went back into the city again and looked for anyone he knew, but failed to find anyone. He said, “Blessed are you, Lord, for great bewilderment has fallen upon me.” He went out again, far from the city, and sat grieving, not knowing where to go. He set down that basket of figs and said, “I will stay here until God takes this bewilderment away from me.”

After he had sat there, he saw an elderly man coming in from the field. Abimelech said to him, “To you I speak, old man: what city is this?” The old man said to him, “It is Jerusalem.”

Abimelech said to him, “Where are Jeremiah the priest, Baruch the Levite, and all the people of this city? For I have found none of them.”

The old man said to him, “Are you not from this city? Is it only now that you remember Jeremiah and ask about him, after you have lived all these days? Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people, for he was taken captive and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia. He went there to prophesy to them.”

When Abimelech heard this from that old man, he said to him, “If you were not an elderly man, I would insult you and laugh at you. But it is not right for people to despise an elderly man. If that were not so, I would say, ‘You have forgotten.’ As for your saying that the people were taken captive to Babylon, even if a mighty heavenly storm had fallen upon them, there would not have been time for them to go to Babylon. Yet you say that they have been taken captive to Babylon!

“As for me, when my father Jeremiah sent me, I went to Agrippa's vineyard for a few figs to give to the sick among the people. I went and reached that place, took what he had commanded me to take, and turned back. As I was going, I found a tree and sat beneath it to shelter in its shade, for it was noon. There I leaned against the basket of figs and slept. When I awoke, it seemed to me that I had dozed. I opened this basket of figs and found them dripping milky sap, just as when I picked them myself. And now you say, ‘The people have been taken captive to Babylon.’ Look and see that even the figs have not withered.”

He opened the basket of figs for him and showed him. The old man looked and saw that the figs were fresh and dripping milky sap. Then that old man marveled and said to Abimelech, “You are righteous, my son, for God did not wish you to see the city's ruin. God brought consolation upon you and preserved your life. Look, today it has been sixty-six years since the day the people were taken captive to Babylon. If you wish to know and be certain, my son, look and see in the fields how their crops have sprouted, and that it is not the season for figs.”

He realized that it was not the season for all this. Then Abimelech said in a loud voice, “I bless you, Lord my God, God of heaven and earth, the rest of the souls of the righteous in all places.”

He said to the old man, “What month is this?” He said to him, “It is the twelfth of the month of Nisan, which is Miyazya.”

After this, Abimelech gave that old man some of these figs and said to him, “May God guide you to the city of Jerusalem above.”

Part 6.

Abimelech rose and went outside the city and prayed to God. And look, an angel came and led him to Baruch, whom he found living among the tombs. When they greeted one another, they wept together and kissed one another. He saw the figs in his basket, lifted his eyes to heaven, and prayed, saying, “Great is God, who gives his righteous ones their reward! Stir yourself, my soul, and rejoice, as you tell the body of flesh [?] the holy house. Your [?] will return into light, and afterward the Faithful One will come and bring you back into your body. Look upon the virginity of your faith, and believe, so that you may live. Look upon these figs: it has been sixty-six years since they were picked, yet they have neither spoiled nor rotted, but are dripping their milky sap even now. So it will be done to you, my flesh, because you have kept the commandment given to you by the angel of righteousness. He who guarded the basket of figs will also guard you by his power.”

When Baruch had said this, Abimelech answered and said to him, “Get up. Let us pray again, so that the Lord may show us the words we should write to Jeremiah in Babylon concerning the shelter with which he sheltered me.”

Baruch prayed and said, “God the Lord is my strength, and the light that comes out of his mouth. Come quickly, I beg you, and I appeal to your goodness. Your name is great, and no one can comprehend it. Listen to the prayer of your servant, so that your will may be known in my heart, that I may carry it out and send it to your priest Jeremiah in Babylon.”

While he was praying this, an angel came and said to him, “Baruch, counselor of light, do not worry about how you will send a message to Jeremiah. Tomorrow, at the hour of light, an eagle will come to you. Consider for yourself the matter of Jeremiah, write it in a letter, and say this to the children of Israel: ‘Whoever is a foreigner among you must separate himself and remain alone for fifteen days. After this I will bring you into the city, says the Lord. Whoever has not separated himself within fifteen days [?] from Babylon, Jeremiah will enter the city and rebuke the people of Babylon, says the Lord.’”

After saying this, the angel departed from Baruch, and Baruch accompanied him as far as the open square. He brought paper and ink and wrote, saying, “From Baruch, the servant of God, who writes a letter to Jeremiah in captivity in Babylon: joy and gladness! For God does not leave us to go out grieving amid affliction and ruin. Because of this, the Lord has shown mercy on our tears and remembered the covenant he previously made with our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

“He sent his angel to me and told me these things, which I am sending to you. These are the things that the Lord, the God of Israel, did, who brought us out of the fiery land of Egypt: ‘Because you did not keep all his righteous ordinances, but exalted your glory and stiffened your necks before him, he handed you over to the furnace of Babylon, because you did not listen to my voice,’ said God through the mouth of Jeremiah, his child. ‘Those who listen, I will bring out of Babylon, and they will no longer be exiles from Jerusalem in Babylon. If you wish to recognize them and examine them, test them with the water of the Jordan. Whoever does not listen will be recognized by the sign of this mark, which is greater than a seal.’”

Part 7.

After writing this, Baruch rose and went out from the tombs. The eagle said to him, “Greetings to you, Baruch, steward of faith.” Baruch said to him, “You are chosen out of all the birds of heaven, for you speak. You can be recognized by the light of your eyes. Now show me why you are staying here.”

The eagle said to him, “I have been sent here so that you may send me with whatever message you wish.” Baruch said to him, “Can you deliver these words to Jeremiah in Babylon?” The eagle said to him, “For this I was sent.”

Baruch took the letter and fifteen figs from that basket of figs which Abimelech had brought, and tied them around the eagle's neck. He said to him, “To you I speak, eagle, king of all the birds: go in peace and life, and bring us news. Do not be like the raven which Noah sent out and which refused to return to him again. Instead, be like the dove which brought word back to Noah three times. Likewise, you too, take these good words to Jeremiah and to the Israelites who are with him, so that it may go well with you. Take this joy to the people chosen by God.

“Even if all the birds and all the enemies of righteousness surround you, wishing to kill you, hurry onward, and the Lord will give you strength. Do not turn to the right or to the left, but go by God's power like an arrow flying straight.”

When Baruch had said this, the eagle flew off with the letter and went to Babylon. He rested on a pillar outside the city, in a deserted place, and waited there until Jeremiah and other people should pass by. They passed that way to bury a man who had died, for Jeremiah had asked Nebuchadnezzar, saying, “Give me land where I may bury those of my people,” and he had given it to him.

As they went along weeping over the dead man, they came before that eagle. The eagle cried out in a loud voice and said, “To you I speak, Jeremiah, God's chosen one: go and gather all the people, and let them come here to hear the good news I have brought.”

When he heard this, he praised God. Then he gathered all the people, their wives, and their children, and they came to where the eagle was. That eagle came down to the dead body and touched it, and it came to life. He did this so that they would believe, and all the people marveled at what had happened. They said, “Surely this is God, who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness with Moses. He has taken the form of an eagle and appeared to us like a great eagle.”

The eagle spoke to Jeremiah, saying, “Come and listen to this letter, and read it to the people.” He read it to them. When the people heard it, they all wept together, put dust on their heads, and said to Jeremiah, “Save us! What should we do to return to our city?”

Jeremiah rose and said to them, “Do everything you heard in the letter, and he will bring you back into your city.”

Jeremiah wrote a letter to Baruch, saying this: “My beloved son, do not grow weary of praying and appealing to God for us, so that he may guide us on our way until we depart by the command of this sinful king. You have found righteousness before God, who did not allow you to come with us, so that you would not see the evil done to the people in Babylon.

“It is like a father who has an only child, and that child is handed over to be punished. Those who are with the father to comfort him cover their faces, so that they do not see his father brought low by grief. In the same way God has shown mercy to you and did not allow you to come to Babylon, so that you would not see the people's suffering.

“For since the day we reached this city, we have had no rest from grief until today—sixty-six years today. As we search, we find people hung up by King Nebuchadnezzar, weeping and saying, ‘Have mercy on us, god Sor.’ When I heard these words, I grieved and wept, as those who were hung up called upon another god and said, ‘Have mercy on us.’ Again I remember the festival we celebrated in Jerusalem before we were taken captive. When I remember, I return to my house in anguish and weeping.

“Now, where you are, you and Abimelech, plead with our God for the people, so that they may listen to my voice and the words of my mouth and depart from Persia. Now I tell you that throughout all the days we have lived here, they have held us, saying, ‘Sing us a new song from the songs of Zion, a song of your God.’ We say to them, ‘How can we sing for you while we are in a foreign land?’”

After Jeremiah had written this, he tied his letter around the eagle's neck and said to him, “Go in peace, and may the Lord watch over you.” The eagle went and flew away and delivered the letter to Baruch. Baruch took the letter and read it, and wept when he heard of the people's pain and suffering.

Jeremiah took those figs and gave them to the sick among the people. He remained, teaching them not to follow the practices of the people of Babylon.

Part 8.

When the day came on which God would bring the people out of Babylon, the Lord said to Jeremiah, “Rise, you and your people, and come to the Jordan. Say to the people, ‘The Lord wishes to put away the practices of the people of Babylon. As for the men among you who have married wives from them, and the women who have married men from them, let us test them.’ Those who listen to you I will bring back into Jerusalem, but those who do not listen to you, do not allow them to enter it.”

Jeremiah spoke all this to them in this way and brought them to the Jordan to test them. As he told them these words which the Lord had spoken to him, those who had married doubted and did not wish to listen to Jeremiah. Some said to him, “We will never abandon our wives. We will take them with us into our city.” They crossed the Jordan and reached Jerusalem.

Jeremiah, Baruch, and Abimelech stood there, saying, “No man who has married someone from Babylon may enter our city.” Those who had married wives said to their companions, “Get up; let us return to Babylon.” They went away and returned.

When the people of Babylon saw them, they came out to refuse them admission and did not allow them to enter Babylon, saying, “You were the first to hate us, and you left us secretly. Therefore you may not enter our city, for we have sworn by the name of our god not to receive you or your daughters, because you departed from us secretly.”

When they heard this, they returned to Jerusalem and built cities for themselves in the regions around Jerusalem. They named that city Samaria. Jeremiah sent word to them, saying, “Repent, and look, the angel of righteousness will come and bring you back to your exalted place.”

Part 9.

They remained rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people for seven days. On the tenth day after this had happened, Jeremiah offered a sacrifice alone.

Jeremiah prayed, saying, “Holy, holy, holy are you, a sweet fragrance to humanity and the true light that shines upon me until I come before you. I plead with you for your people, and I ask you by the melodious voice of the seraphim and by the fragrance of the cherubim's incense. I ask you, yes, [?] singer Michael, the angel of righteousness, who opens the gates of righteousness so that they may enter them. I plead with you, Lord of all, the Lord who holds everything and created everything, who appears and was not born, who completed everything. All creation is hidden with him before it is made in secret.”

He prayed this, and when he had finished his prayer, Jeremiah stood in the temple, with Baruch and Abimelech beside him. Jeremiah became like a man whose soul had departed from him. Then Baruch and Abimelech fell down and cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Woe to us! Our father Jeremiah, God's priest, has departed from us!”

When the people heard this, they ran to him and found Jeremiah fallen down and dead. They wept, tore their clothes, put dust on their heads, and wept bitterly. After they had prepared to bury him, a voice came, saying, “Do not wrap him for burial. He is alive, and his soul will return to his body again.”

When they heard this voice, they did not wrap him for burial, but remained around him, watching over him for three days until his soul returned to his body. A voice sounded among them all and said, “Praise him with one voice! Praise God, and all of you praise the Messiah, the Son of God, who will awaken you and judge you: Jesus, the Son of God, the light of the whole world, the lamp that does not go out, and the life of faith.

“After these days there will be three hundred and three weeks of days until his coming to earth. The tree of life, which is in the garden and was not planted, will cause all trees that bear fruit, and the dry trees, to come to him. He will make them bear fruit and sprout, and their fruit will remain with the angels. For the planting of the trees, so that they may flourish and grow, let us give dew to the air, so that their roots do not dry up like a plant whose roots have not taken hold of the earth.

“Those that are red in color will become white like wool. Sweet water will become bitter, and bitter water will become sweet, with great gladness. God's joys will be for the barren, so that they bear fruit by the word of his mouth, his Son. He himself will enter the world and choose twelve apostles for himself, so that what I saw may be shown to them: the adorned one who is sent from his Father, who comes into the world, walks upon the Mount of Olives, and satisfies the hungry soul.”

Jeremiah spoke in this way about the Son of God, that he would come into the world. When the people heard this, they were angry about it and said, “These are the words of Isaiah son of Amoz, who says, ‘I saw God, the Son of God.’ Now get up; let us do to him what we did to Isaiah.” Some of them said, “No! Rather, let us stone him.”

Baruch and Abimelech cried out to them, saying, “Do not kill him with this death!” Baruch and Abimelech grieved for Jeremiah, and they still did not let him tell them the hidden things he had seen.

Jeremiah said to them, “Be quiet; do not weep, for they cannot kill me until I tell you everything I have seen. Now bring me one stone.” They brought him one stone. He set it upright and said, “Eternal light, make this stone have the appearance of a human being.” Then the stone took on Jeremiah's appearance and resembled him. They began to stone the stone, thinking it was Jeremiah himself.

Jeremiah told Baruch and Abimelech all the hidden things he had seen. After he had finished telling them, he went and stood among the people, wishing to complete his course. Then that stone cried out to them and said, “Foolish children of Israel, why do you stone me, thinking I am Jeremiah? Look, Jeremiah is standing among you!”

When they saw him, they rushed upon him with many stones and completed their lawless deed. They buried him, took that stone and set it in his tomb, and made it like a door. They wrote on it, saying, ‘Look, this is Jeremiah's helper.’

Section 4.

On the second day, at dawn, the army of the Chaldeans surrounded the city. A great angel blew a horn and said, “Enter, army of the Chaldeans! Look, the gates are being opened for you.” Then the king entered with his army, and they took all the people captive.

Then Jeremiah took the keys of the temple, went outside the city, and threw these keys toward the sun, saying, “To you I speak, sun! Take the keys of the house of God and keep them until the time when the Lord asks you for them. For our generation was not worthy to keep them, since we were found to be shameless in our sin.” While Jeremiah was weeping for the people, they brought him out, [?], and drove him with the people as far as Babylon.

But Baruch took dust, put it on his head, sat down, and uttered this lament: “Why was Jerusalem destroyed, if not because of the sin of the beloved people? She was handed over to her enemies because of our sin and that of the people. But let the sinners not boast and say, ‘We were able to take the city of God by our own strength.’ It was not by your might that you overcame her; rather, she was handed over to you because of our sin. Our God will have mercy on us and bring us back to our city, but for you there is no life. Blessed are our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, because they departed from this world and did not see the destruction of this city.”

After saying this, he went out weeping and said, “I grieve for you, Jerusalem.” He left the city and stayed among the tombs, and angels would come and tell him about everything.

Part 5.

Abimelech brought figs at noon from the place to which Jeremiah had sent him. He found a leafy tree and sat in its shade to rest a little. He rested his head on the basket of figs and slept for sixty-six years without waking from his sleep.

After these days, he got up and awoke from his sleep. He said, “I wish I could sleep a little longer, because my head is still heavy and I have not had enough sleep.” He opened the basket of figs and found that the figs were fresh and dripping milky sap. He wanted to sleep again because his head was heavy and he had not had enough sleep. But he said, “I am afraid to sleep or doze, lest my father Jeremiah rebuke me, because he sent me off in a hurry this morning. Now I will get up and go, because the heat is intense and does not let up anywhere.”

He got up, took his basket of figs, and entered the city of Jerusalem. He did not recognize the city or his house. He said, “Blessed are you, Lord!” For great bewilderment had come upon him. He said, “Is this not the city of Jerusalem? Perhaps I am mistaken because I came by the mountain road. Or perhaps it is because my head is heavy, I have not had enough sleep, and my mind has forgotten. How can I tell Jeremiah about this—that the city has become strange to me?”

He searched for every landmark in the city to find out whether it was indeed Jerusalem. He went back into the city and looked for anyone he knew, but found no one. He said, “Blessed are you, Lord, for great bewilderment has come upon me!” He went out of the city again, a long way off, and sat down, grieving and not knowing where to go. He set down the basket of figs and said, “I will sit here until God removes this distress from me.”

After he had sat there, he saw an old man coming in from the field. Abimelech said to him, “You there, old man, I am speaking to you: what city is this?” The old man said to him, “It is Jerusalem.”

Abimelech said to him, “Where are Jeremiah the priest, Baruch the Levite, and all the people of this city? I have found none of them.”

The old man said to him, “Are you not from this city? And do you only now remember Jeremiah and ask about him, after living all these days? Jeremiah is in Babylon with the people, because he was taken captive and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Persia. He went there to prophesy to them.”

When Abimelech heard this from the old man, he said to him, “If you were not an old man, I would have insulted you and laughed at you. But one must not treat people, or an old man, with contempt. If that were not so, I would have said, ‘You are out of your mind!’ As for your saying that the people were taken captive to Babylon—even if a great downpour from heaven had fallen upon them, there would not have been time for them to go to Babylon. Yet you say they have been taken captive to Babylon!

“As for me, my father Jeremiah sent me, and I went to Agrippa’s vineyard for a few figs to give to the sick among the people. I went and arrived there, took what he had ordered me to take, and returned. As I was walking, I found a tree and sat beneath it in the shade, because it was noon. There I rested my head on the basket of figs and slept. When I woke, it seemed to me that I had only dozed. I opened this basket of figs and found them dripping milky sap, just as when I picked them. Yet here you are saying that the people have been taken captive to Babylon! Look: even the figs have not withered.”

He opened the basket of figs for him and showed him. The old man looked and saw that the figs were fresh and dripping milky sap. Then the old man was astonished and said to Abimelech, “You are righteous, my son, because God did not wish to show you the destruction of the city. God brought a deep sleep upon you and kept you alive. Look, today it has been sixty-six years since the people were taken captive to Babylon. If you want to know and be certain, my son, look at the fields and see how their crops have sprouted, and that it is not the season for figs.”

He realized that it was not the season for any of these things. Then Abimelech said in a loud voice, “I bless you, Lord my God, God of heaven and earth, the resting place of the souls of the righteous wherever they go!”

He said to the old man, “What month is this?” He said to him, “It is the twelfth of the month of Nisan, which is Miyazya.”

After this, Abimelech gave the old man some of the figs and said to him, “May God lead you to the city of Jerusalem above.”

Chapter 6.

Abimelech rose and went outside the city and prayed to God. And behold, an angel came and led him to Baruch, whom he found sitting in a tomb. When they greeted one another, they wept together and kissed one another. Baruch saw the figs in his basket, raised his eyes to heaven, and prayed, saying:

“Great is God, who gives his righteous people their reward! Leap, my soul, and rejoice as you speak to the body of flesh [?] the holy house. Your moisture will turn into light, and afterward the faithful one will come and bring you back into your body. Look upon the virginity of your faith, and believe that you will live. Look at [?] the figs! Behold, it has been sixty-six years since they were picked, yet they have neither decayed nor gone bad. Instead, their milky juice still drips to this day. So it will be done to you, my flesh, because you have kept the command given you by the angel of righteousness. He who preserved the basket of figs will also preserve you by his power.”

When Baruch had said this, Abimelech answered him, “Rise, and let us pray again, so that the Lord may show us the words we should write to Jeremiah in Babylon about the protection with which he covered me.”

Baruch prayed and said, “My strength is God the Lord, and the light that comes from his mouth. First I implore you and take refuge in your goodness. Your name is great, and no one can comprehend it. Hear the prayer of your servant, so that your will may be known in my heart, that I may do it and send it to your priest Jeremiah in Babylon.”

As he prayed this, an angel came and said to him, “Baruch, counselor of light, do not worry about how you are to send a message to Jeremiah. Tomorrow, at the hour of daylight, an eagle will come to you. You yourself must consider the matter of Jeremiah and write it in a letter. Say this to the children of Israel: ‘Whoever is a foreigner among you must separate himself and remain alone for fifteen days. Afterward I will bring you into the city, says the Lord. Whoever has not separated himself within fifteen days [?]. Jeremiah will come from Babylon into the city and rebuke the people of Babylon, says the Lord.’”

After saying this, the angel departed from Baruch. Baruch accompanied him as far as the square, then brought paper and ink and wrote, saying:

“From Baruch, the servant of God, who writes a letter to Jeremiah in the fortress of Babylon: Joy and gladness! For God has not abandoned us to depart in sorrow amid wrath and decay. Therefore the Lord has had compassion on our tears and remembered the covenant he established long ago with our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

“He sent his angel to me and told me these things that I have sent to you. These are the things that the Lord, the God of Israel, has done, who brought us out of the fiery land of Egypt: ‘Because you did not keep all his righteous ordinances, but exalted your honor and stiffened your necks before him, he handed you over to the furnace of Babylon, because you did not listen to my voice,’ said God through the mouth of Jeremiah, his child.

“Those who listen, I will bring out of Babylon, and they will no longer be exiles from Jerusalem in Babylon. If you wish to recognize them and examine them, test them with the water of the Jordan. Whoever does not listen will be recognized by this sign, which is greater than a seal.”

Chapter 7.

Baruch rose and, having written this, came out of the tomb. The eagle said to him, “Greetings, Baruch, guardian of the faith!” Baruch said to it, “You are chosen from among all the birds of heaven, for you can speak. You are recognizable by the brightness of your eyes. Now tell me why you are staying here.”

The eagle said to him, “I have been sent here so that you may send me with whatever message you wish.”

Baruch said to it, “Can you carry a message and deliver it to Jeremiah in Babylon?”

The eagle said to him, “For this purpose I was sent.”

Baruch took a letter and fifteen figs from the basket of figs that Abimelech had brought, and tied them around the eagle’s neck. He said to it, “I say to you, eagle, king of all the birds: go in peace and in safety, and bring us news. Do not be like the raven that Noah sent out, which refused to return to him again. Instead, be like the dove that brought a message back to Noah three times. Likewise, take these good words to Jeremiah and to the Israelites who are with him, so that it may go well with you. Take this joy to the people chosen by God. Even if all the birds and all the enemies of righteousness surround you, wishing to kill you, hurry onward, and the Lord will give you strength. Do not turn to the right or to the left, but go in the strength of God, like an arrow that flies straight.”

When Baruch had said this, the eagle flew away with the letter and went to Babylon. It rested on a pillar outside the city, in a deserted place, and waited there until Jeremiah and other people should pass by. They passed that way to bury a man who had died, for Jeremiah had asked Nebuchadnezzar, saying, “Give me some land where I may bury people from among my people,” and he had given it to him.

As they walked, weeping over the dead man, they came before the eagle. The eagle cried out in a loud voice and said, “To you I speak, Jeremiah, chosen one of God! Go and gather all the people, and let them come here to hear the good news I have brought.”

When he heard this, he praised God. At once he gathered all the people, their wives, and their children, and they came to where the eagle was. The eagle came down to the corpse and touched it, and the dead man came to life. It did this so that they would believe. All the people marveled at what had happened. They said, “Indeed, this is God, who appeared to our fathers in the wilderness with Moses. He has taken the form of an eagle and appeared to us as a great eagle.”

The eagle said to Jeremiah, “Come and hear this letter, and read it to the people.” He read it to them. When the people heard it, they all wept together and put dust on their heads. They said to Jeremiah, “Save us! What must we do to return to our city?”

Jeremiah stood up and said to them, “Do everything you have heard in the letter, and he will bring you back to your city.”

Jeremiah wrote a letter to Baruch as follows:

“My beloved son, do not grow weary of prayer as you plead with God for us, so that he may guide us on our way until we leave by the command of this sinful king. You have found favor before God, who did not allow you to come with us, so that you would not see the evil being done to the people in Babylon.

“It is like a father who has an only child, and that child is handed over to be punished. Those who are with his father, comforting him, cover their faces so that they may not see the father brought low by grief. In the same way, God had mercy on you and did not allow you to come to Babylon, so that you would not see the people’s distress.

“For from the day we arrived in this city until today, we have had no rest from sorrow—sixty-six years now. As we search, we find people hung up by King Nebuchadnezzar, weeping and saying, ‘Have mercy on us, god Sor!’ When I heard these words, I grieved and wept, as those who were hung up called upon another god and said, ‘Have mercy on us!’ Again I remember the festival we celebrated in Jerusalem, without our calling out [?]. Remembering it, I return to my house in anguish and tears.

“Now, wherever you are, you and Abimelech, plead with our God for the people, so that they may listen to my voice and the words of my mouth, and come out of Persia.

“And now I tell you: throughout all the days we have stayed here, they have seized us, saying, ‘Give us a new song from the songs of Zion, a song of your God.’ We say to them, ‘How can we sing for you while we are in a foreign land?’”

After writing this, Jeremiah tied his letter around the eagle’s neck and said to it, “Go in peace, and may the Lord watch over you.”

The eagle departed and flew away, delivering the letter to Baruch. Baruch took the letter and read it, and he wept when he heard of the people’s suffering and distress.

Jeremiah took the figs and gave them to the sick among the people. He remained there, teaching them not to follow the practices of the people of Babylon.

Chapter 8.

When the day arrived on which God would bring the people out of Babylon, the Lord said to Jeremiah, “Rise, you and your people, and come to the Jordan. Tell the people: ‘The Lord wishes to cover over the deeds of the people of Babylon. As for the men among you who have married women, and the women who have married men from among them, let us test them. Bring those who obey you into Jerusalem, but do not allow those who do not obey you to enter it.’”

Jeremiah told them all this and brought them to the Jordan to test them. While he was telling them these words that the Lord had spoken to him, those who had married wavered and refused to obey Jeremiah. Some said to him, “We will never abandon our wives. We will take them with us into our city.” They crossed the Jordan and reached Jerusalem.

Jeremiah, Baruch, and Abimelech stood there, saying, “No man who has married a woman from Babylon may enter our city.” Those who had married women said to their companions, “Rise, let us return to Babylon.” They went back.

When the people of Babylon saw them, they came out to refuse them admission and would not let them enter Babylon. They said, “You hated us before and secretly departed from us. Therefore you may not enter our city, for we have sworn in the name of our god that we will not receive you or your daughters, because you secretly left us.”

When they heard this, they returned to Jerusalem and built themselves cities in the regions around Jerusalem. They named that city Samaria. Jeremiah sent word to them, saying, “Repent and [?]. An angel of righteousness will come and bring you back to your spacious place.”

Chapter 9.

They remained there rejoicing and offering sacrifices for the people for seven days. On the tenth day after this happened, Jeremiah offered a sacrifice by himself. Jeremiah prayed, saying, “Holy, holy, holy! You are a sweet fragrance to humanity and the true light that shines for me until I come before you. I plead with you for your people, and I ask you by the harmonious voice of the seraphim and by the fragrance of the cherubim’s incense. I ask you—yes, Michael the singer is the angel of righteousness who opens the gates of righteousness so that they may enter them. I plead with you, Lord of all, Lord who holds everything and created everything, who appears and was not born, who completed everything. All creation is hidden with him before things are made in secret.”

He prayed this, and when he had finished his prayer, Jeremiah stood in the temple, with Baruch and Abimelech beside him. Jeremiah became like a man whose soul had departed from him. Then Baruch and Abimelech fell down and cried out loudly, saying, “Woe to us! Our father Jeremiah, the priest of God, has departed from us!”

When the people heard this, they ran to him and found Jeremiah fallen down and dead. They wept, tore their clothes, put dust on their heads, and wept bitterly. After they had prepared to bury him, a voice came, saying, “Do not wrap him for burial. He is alive, and his soul will return to his body again.” When they heard this voice, they did not wrap him for burial. Instead, they remained around him, keeping watch for three days until his soul returned to his body.

A voice sounded among them all and said, “Praise him with one voice! Praise God! All of you, praise the Messiah, the Son of God, who will awaken you and judge you: Jesus, the Son of God, the light of the whole world, the lamp that does not go out, and the life of faith.

“After this there will be three hundred days and three weeks of days until his coming to earth. The tree of life, which is in paradise and was not planted, will cause all the trees that bear fruit, and the dry trees, to come to him. He will make them bear fruit and sprout, and their fruit will remain with the angels. For the planted trees to flourish and grow tall, morning dew will be given to [?], so that their roots will not dry up like a plant whose root has not taken hold of the ground. What is red in color will be made white like wool. Sweet water will become bitter, and bitter water will become sweet, with great rejoicing. God’s joys will be for the islands, so that they may bear fruit through the word of his mouth, his Son.

“He himself will enter the world and choose twelve apostles for himself, so that what I saw may be shown to them: the glorious one who is sent from his Father and comes into the world. He will go to the Mount of Olives and satisfy the hungry soul.”

This is how Jeremiah spoke about the Son of God coming into the world. When the people heard this, they became angry about it and said, “These are the words of Isaiah son of Amoz, who says, ‘I have seen God, the Son of God.’ Now get up! Let us do to him what we did to Isaiah.” Half of them said, “No! Rather, let us stone him.”

Baruch and Abimelech cried out to them, saying, “Do not kill him with this kind of death!” Baruch and Abimelech grieved over Jeremiah. Moreover, the people did not allow him to tell them the hidden things he had seen. Jeremiah said to them, “Be quiet. Do not weep, for they cannot kill me until I have told you everything I saw. Now bring me a stone.”

They brought him a stone, and he set it up and said, “Everlasting light, make this stone take on the appearance of a human being.” Immediately the stone took on Jeremiah’s appearance and resembled him. They began to stone the stone, thinking it was Jeremiah himself.

Jeremiah told Baruch and Abimelech all the hidden things he had seen. After he had finished telling them, he went and stood among the people, wishing to complete his ministry. Then that stone cried out to them and said, “You foolish children of Israel! Why are you stoning me, thinking that I am Jeremiah himself? Look, Jeremiah is standing among you!”

When they saw him, they ran with many stones and completed their transgression. They buried him, took that stone, and placed it in his tomb, making it serve as a door. They wrote on it, saying, “Look, this is Jeremiah’s disciple.”
